props.title: The Fog of War
props.initialSlug: The Fog of War: Clarity Unveiled

sections.content: The Fog of War (2003) revolutionized documentary filmmaking through Errol Morris's innovative Interrotron interview technique, capturing Robert McNamara's unflinching gaze as he dissects the Vietnam War's catastrophic decisions. Morris structures the film around McNamara's 11 lessons from warfare, creating a masterclass in both historical documentation and visual storytelling. The film's hypnotic Philip Glass score and striking archival footage manipulation technique influenced countless documentaries like Standard Operating Procedure (2008) and The Unknown Known (2013), establishing a new standard for political documentary storytelling.

sections.content: Morris's approach spawned a wave of political documentaries that prioritize intimate access to power players. The Unknown Known (2013) applied similar techniques to Donald Rumsfeld, while The Act of Killing (2012) pushed even further by having Indonesian death squad leaders reenact their crimes. These films share Morris's core insight: let powerful figures reveal themselves through extended conversation rather than narrative voiceover.

The film's innovative use of archival footage, particularly the haunting sequences of bombing runs set to Glass's minimalist score, influenced visual storytelling across genres. Operation Overlord (1975) and Why We Fight (2005) both borrowed Morris's technique of repurposing military footage to critique war itself, while The Look of Silence (2014) adopted his intimate interview style to confront genocide perpetrators. sections.content: Contemporary filmmakers continue building on Morris's foundation. The Act of Killing (2012) director Joshua Oppenheimer explicitly credits The Fog of War for showing how to engage with morally compromised subjects, while Standard Operating Procedure (2008) applies Morris's techniques to the Abu Ghraib scandal. The film's influence extends beyond subject matter into technical innovation - Morris's Interrotron interview system, which allows subjects to make eye contact with viewers while being interviewed, has become standard documentary practice.
